elements.element: The Agreement is governed by the laws of the State of New York.
elements.evidence: Section 15.9 expressly selects the internal laws of the State of Delaware, not New York.

elements.element: The state courts located in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction.
elements.evidence: Section 15.10.1 instead selects the state courts located in Delaware. The New York arbitral seat does not establish New York court jurisdiction.

elements.element: The federal courts located in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction.
elements.evidence: Section 15.10.1 instead selects the federal courts located in Delaware. The New York arbitral seat does not establish New York court jurisdiction.

elements.element: The Agreement is governed by Delaware law, California law, or the laws of England and Wales.
elements.evidence: Section 15.9 expressly provides that the Agreement is governed by the internal laws of Delaware, an accepted fallback jurisdiction.

elements.element: Disputes are submitted to the courts of the selected fallback jurisdiction—Delaware or California courts, or London courts where England and Wales law applies—rather than mandatory pre-dispute arbitration.
elements.evidence: For the selected Delaware-law alternative, Section 15.10.1 generally requires unresolved Disputes to be resolved exclusively by Delaware state and federal courts. Sections 15.10.2.1 and 15.10.2.2 permit arbitration only if both Parties agree in writing after the Dispute arises, so arbitration is not mandatory. The retained IP, Material Impact, and preliminary-injunction provisions operate as express exceptions to the general forum provision.

result.reason: The redline does not satisfy the New York preferred position, but it reaches the Delaware fallback by retaining Delaware governing law and replacing mandatory arbitration with Delaware court litigation as the default. The changes are confined to the dispute-resolution mechanism and preserve the existing escalation process and express carve-outs. Drafting quality is reduced because the retained sentence assigning disputes over the propriety of commencing arbitration to the arbitral tribunal is awkward alongside the requirement for mutual post-dispute written consent, and the IP carve-out permits an unspecified U.S. federal court rather than expressly requiring a Delaware federal court.
